preamble.summary: Solomon's great prayer for wisdom. He addresses God as the Creator who made all things by his word and formed the human being by his wisdom to have dominion over creation. He confesses his own weakness and asks God to send wisdom from the holy heavens and from the throne of glory to labor alongside him. For the reasoning of mortals is feeble and the body weighs down the soul. Only through wisdom sent from above can anyone know God's will.
preamble.remarkable: This is the most sustained prayer in the deuterocanonical wisdom literature and one of the finest prayers in all of Scripture. Verse 15 ('the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly tent burdens the thoughtful mind') became one of the most quoted verses in patristic theology and directly influenced 2 Corinthians 5:1-4. The prayer's structure -- invocation, confession of weakness, petition, theological reasoning -- became a model for Christian liturgical prayer.
preamble.friction: Verse 15's language about the body weighing down the soul echoes Platonic dualism (especially Plato's Phaedo), and the tension between this anthropology and the more integrated Hebrew view of the person is palpable. The author seems to adopt Platonic vocabulary while attempting to maintain a biblical theology of creation as good.
preamble.connections: 1 Kings 3:6-9 (Solomon's prayer at Gibeon); Psalm 104 (God the Creator); Proverbs 8:27-30 (Wisdom present at creation); 2 Corinthians 5:1-4 (earthly tent/heavenly dwelling); Romans 11:33-34 (who has known the mind of the Lord?).

verses.text_latin: Deus patrum meorum et Domine misericordiae qui fecisti omnia verbo tuo.
verses.rendering: O God of my fathers, and Lord of mercy, who made all things by your word.
translator_notes: The prayer opens with three titles: God of the patriarchs (historical continuity), Lord of mercy (character), Creator by word (power). The phrase 'by your word' (verbo tuo) echoes Genesis 1 ('And God said') and anticipates John 1:3 ('All things came into being through him').

key_terms.note: The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; Solomon anchors his prayer in covenantal history.
The creative Word (verbum/logos) through which all things were made; a bridge between Genesis 1 and John 1.

verses.text_latin: Et sapientia tua constituisti hominem ut dominaretur creaturae quae a te facta est.
verses.rendering: And by your wisdom formed the human being, to have dominion over the creatures you have made.
translator_notes: Word and Wisdom are parallel agents of creation. The human vocation is dominion (Genesis 1:26-28), but this dominion is itself the product of wisdom, not raw power.

key_terms.note: Wisdom as co-agent of creation; paired with 'word' in v. 1, the two become virtually interchangeable.
From dominari, to rule; echoes Genesis 1:26-28, but the context of wisdom reframes dominion as stewardship.

verses.text_latin: Ut disponat orbem terrarum in aequitate et iustitia et in directione cordis iudicium iudicet.
verses.rendering: To govern the world in equity and justice, and to pronounce judgment with an upright heart.
translator_notes: Human governance is defined by three qualities: equity (fairness), justice (right order), and integrity of heart. Without these, dominion becomes tyranny.

key_terms.note: The twin pillars of right governance; aequitas is fairness in application, iustitia is the principle itself.
Directio cordis means straightness or integrity of heart; the inner character of the judge determines the quality of judgment.

verses.text_latin: Da mihi sedium tuarum adsistiricem sapientiam et noli me reprobare a pueris tuis.
verses.rendering: Give me the wisdom that sits beside your throne, and do not reject me from among your servants.
translator_notes: The central petition. Wisdom 'sits beside' God's throne (adsistrix, the feminine form of 'one who stands/sits beside'), sharing God's sovereign perspective. Solomon asks to share in that perspective.

key_terms.rendered_as: the wisdom that sits beside your throne
key_terms.note: Wisdom as royal consort seated at God's side; she shares in his governance and perspective.
Literally 'your children'; Solomon identifies himself as God's servant/child, dependent on divine favor.

verses.text_latin: Quoniam servus tuus sum ego et filius ancillae tuae, homo infirmus et exigui temporis et minor ad intellectum iudicii et legum.
verses.rendering: For I am your servant, the son of your handmaid, a person who is weak and short-lived, with little understanding of judgment and laws.
translator_notes: The self-abasement is conventional but sincere. Solomon claims no inherent qualification for rule. The phrase 'son of your handmaid' (filius ancillae tuae) echoes Psalm 116:16 and signals total dependence on God.

key_terms.rendered_as: a person who is weak and short-lived
key_terms.note: Solomon returns to the theme of chapter 7: the king is a mortal, limited in both strength and time.

verses.text_latin: Nam et si quis erit consummatus inter filios hominum, si ab illo abfuerit sapientia tua, in nihilum computabitur.
verses.rendering: For even if one is perfect among the children of mortals, without your wisdom that person will be regarded as nothing.
translator_notes: The universal principle: human perfection without divine wisdom equals zero. No natural endowment can substitute for the gift of God.

verses.text_latin: Tu me elegisti regem populo tuo et iudicem filiorum tuorum et filiarum.
verses.rendering: You chose me to be king of your people, and judge over your sons and daughters.
translator_notes: Solomon's kingship is explicitly grounded in divine election, not hereditary right or popular acclaim.

key_terms.note: The people of Israel are God's children; the king rules God's family, not his own subjects.

verses.text_latin: Et dixisti me aedificare templum in monte sancto tuo et in civitate habitationis tuae altare similitudinem tabernaculi sancti tui quod praeparasti ab initio.
verses.rendering: You commanded me to build a temple on your holy mountain, and an altar in the city of your dwelling, a copy of the holy tabernacle that you prepared from the beginning.
translator_notes: The earthly temple is a 'copy' (similitudinem) of a heavenly original. This Platonic-sounding idea has deep roots in Exodus 25:9, 40 ('according to the pattern shown you on the mountain') and becomes central to the argument of Hebrews 8-9.

key_terms.rendered_as: a copy of the holy tabernacle
key_terms.note: The earthly temple reproduces a heavenly archetype; worship on earth mirrors worship in heaven.
The heavenly tabernacle precedes creation; it is part of God's original design, not an afterthought.

verses.text_latin: Et tecum sapientia quae novit opera tua, quae et adfuit tunc cum orbem terrarum faceres et sciebat quid esset placitum oculis tuis et quid directum in praeceptis tuis.
verses.rendering: And with you is wisdom, who knows your works, who was present when you made the world, and who understands what is pleasing in your eyes and what is right according to your commandments.
translator_notes: Wisdom's qualifications as counselor: she was present at creation (cf. Proverbs 8:27-30), she knows what pleases God, and she understands his law. No one is better placed to advise the king.

key_terms.latin: adfuit tunc cum orbem terrarum faceres
key_terms.rendered_as: was present when you made the world
key_terms.note: Wisdom's presence at creation is her credential; she knows the Creator's intentions because she watched him work.

verses.text_latin: Mitte illam de caelis sanctis tuis et a sede magnitudinis tuae mitte illam ut mecum sit et mecum laboret ut sciam quid acceptum sit apud te.
verses.rendering: Send her forth from the holy heavens, and from the throne of your majesty send her, that she may labor alongside me, and I may learn what is pleasing to you.
translator_notes: The petition reaches its climax with the double imperative: 'Send her... send her' (mitte... mitte). The repetition expresses urgency. Wisdom descends from heaven to work alongside the king -- she is not a remote principle but a present companion.

key_terms.note: Wisdom's origin is heavenly; she must descend to be available to mortals.
Wisdom is not merely a consultant but a co-worker; she shares in the toil of governance.

verses.text_latin: Scit enim illa omnia et intellegit et deducet me in operibus meis sobrie et custodiet me in sua potentia.
verses.rendering: For she knows and understands all things, and she will guide me prudently in my actions, and will guard me with her splendor.

key_terms.note: Sobrie means with moderation, temperately; wisdom's guidance is measured, not extreme.

verses.text_latin: Et erunt accepta opera mea et disponam populum tuum iuste et ero dignus sedium patris mei.
verses.rendering: Then my works will be acceptable, and I will govern your people justly, and will be worthy of my father's throne.
translator_notes: The prayer's goal is not personal enrichment but worthy governance. Solomon asks for wisdom in order to serve.

key_terms.note: The reference to David's throne links Solomon's prayer to the Davidic covenant and its promises.

verses.text_latin: Quis enim hominum poterit scire consilium Dei? Aut quis poterit cogitare quid velit Deus?
verses.rendering: For what mortal can know the counsel of God? Or who can discern what the Lord wills?
translator_notes: The rhetorical questions shift from petition to theological reflection. The expected answer is 'no one -- unless God reveals it.' This passage is echoed in Romans 11:34 and 1 Corinthians 2:16.

key_terms.note: Consilium is deliberate planning; God's purposes are not arbitrary but planned, yet they exceed human comprehension.

verses.text_latin: Cogitationes enim mortalium timidae et incertae providentiae nostrae.
verses.rendering: For the reasoning of mortals is timid, and our plans are uncertain.
translator_notes: Human reason is not dismissed but acknowledged as limited: timid (timidae) and uncertain (incertae). The problem is not intelligence but finitude.

key_terms.note: Human thoughts are hesitant, lacking the confidence that only divine perspective can provide.

verses.text_latin: Corpus enim quod corrumpitur adgravat animam, et terrena inhabitatio deprimit sensum multa cogitantem.
verses.rendering: For a perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthly tent burdens the thoughtful mind.
translator_notes: One of the most influential verses in the entire deuterocanonical corpus. Paul echoes it in 2 Corinthians 5:1-4 ('we who are in this tent groan, being burdened'). The language is Platonic (the body as impediment to the soul), but the context is creational, not dualistic: the body is 'perishable' (a consequence of the Fall), not inherently evil.

key_terms.note: The body is subject to decay; the qualifier 'quod corrumpitur' (which is being corrupted) suggests that corruption is a condition, not an essence.
Inhabitatio (dwelling place) figures the body as a temporary shelter; the 'tent' metaphor implies transience and suggests a more permanent dwelling to come.
The mind (sensus) is weighed down by embodiment; spiritual insight requires overcoming the limitations of physical existence.

verses.text_latin: Et difficile aestimamus quae in terra sunt et quae in prospectu sunt invenimus cum labore; quae in caelis autem sunt quis investigavit?
verses.rendering: We can scarcely guess at what is on earth, and what is at hand we find with labor; but who has traced out what is in the heavens?
translator_notes: The epistemological humility deepens: if earthly things are hard to know, heavenly things are impossible without divine assistance. The argument builds toward the necessity of revelation.

verses.text_latin: Sensum autem tuum quis sciet nisi tu dederis sapientiam et miseris Spiritum Sanctum tuum de altissimis?
verses.rendering: And who could have known your will, unless you had given wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from on high?
translator_notes: The climactic verse of the prayer. Three agents converge: God's will, wisdom, and the Holy Spirit. The Trinitarian resonance is unmistakable in a Christian reading. The verse answers the questions of vv. 13 and 16: the gap between human limitation and divine purpose is bridged only by God's own initiative.

key_terms.note: The most explicit pneumatological statement in Wisdom; the Holy Spirit is sent from the heights as the agent of revelation.
From the highest places; the Spirit descends from God's own realm to illuminate human minds.

verses.text_latin: Et sic correctae sunt semitae eorum qui sunt in terris et quae tibi placent didicerunt homines.
verses.rendering: And thus the paths of those on earth were set right, and mortals were taught what pleases you.
translator_notes: The prayer concludes with the result of wisdom's descent: straightened paths and true knowledge of God's will. The language echoes Isaiah 40:3 ('make straight in the desert a highway for our God').

key_terms.note: Semita is a narrow path; without wisdom, humanity wanders on crooked trails. Wisdom straightens the way.

verses.text_latin: Et per sapientiam sanati sunt quicumque placuerunt tibi Domine a principio.
verses.rendering: And by wisdom all who have pleased you, O Lord, from the beginning were saved.
translator_notes: The prayer's final word is 'saved' (sanati, literally 'healed'). Wisdom is not merely illumination but salvation. Every righteous person from the beginning of history has been saved through wisdom. This claim sets up the historical review of chapters 10-19.

key_terms.note: Sanare means to heal or make whole; salvation is figured as healing, suggesting that the human condition without wisdom is a form of illness.
Wisdom's saving work extends back to the origin of humanity; she is not a latecomer to the story of redemption.
